notes:
I found enough for useful notes on most verses, but there are real gaps. I ran out of searches before I could check Gill, Ellicott, the Pulpit Commentary, any Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Pentecostal (ag.org) or Orthodox (oca.org) source, the modern scholarship sites (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org), or any prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. Those are left out.

Some sources were only partly readable. The Enduring Word page cut off partway through its notes on v. 12, so for vv. 13–15 I only have the site's AI-written summary, and the Precept Austin page cut off partway through its notes on v. 1. Points I took from the full pages I read (rather than from search snippets) have their URL but no citation tag.

---

**v. 1**
- Wesley says the "therefore" means "seeing God is so gracious." He defines supplication as asking for help in need, prayer as any offering of our desires to God, and intercession is prayer for others. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-timothy-2.html
- Wesley also says we can give thanks for everyone for that God willeth all men to be saved, and Christ is the Mediator of all. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_timothy/2.htm
- Guzik (Enduring Word) says "first of all" is about importance, not order in time. He explains the four kinds of prayer and says praying for "all men" includes enemies and people we're in conflict with, and means praying for the lost. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-2/
- Precept Austin also reads "first" as priority. It says "all men" includes even Hymenaeus and Alexander from chapter 1, but not the dead. It quotes Barclay that few passages stress the gospel's universality as much as this one. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-2-commentary
- Catholic view: Catholic Answers argues that the prayers of v. 1 are acts of mediation. In them Christians act as a *subordinate* mediation by which we participate in the mediation of Jesus Christ. It is a mediation that is effective through, with, and in Christ. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/intercessory-power

**v. 2**
- Guzik notes that early Christians, accused of undermining the state, answered that they prayed *for* the emperor, not *to* him. He says Christians should look for no special favours from government, only to be left free to live their faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-2/
- Wesley says even minor local officials do much good or harm. He glosses "godliness" as inward religion and "honesty" as the whole duty we owe our neighbour. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-timothy-2.html
- Precept Austin says Scripture assigns government the responsibilities of safety, stability, peace, and justice (Romans 13:1–5; 1 Timothy 2:2). https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-2-commentary

**v. 3**
- Wesley says "this" means praying for everyone. To the question of why more people aren't converted, he answers We do not pray enough. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-timothy-2.html

**v. 4: a real divide between traditions**
- *Methodist (Wesley):* God wills seriously all men - Not a part only, much less the smallest part. "To come" means They are not compelled. He finds it strange that anyone God has saved would doubt the universality of his grace! https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-timothy-2.html
- *Calvary Chapel / charismatic (Guzik):* God's desire for all men to be saved is conditioned by His desire to have a genuine response from human beings. So any idea of limiting evangelism to the elect is absurd. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-2/
- *Reformed (John Samson, Monergism):* Reads "all" in context as all types of people.. including these influential people with authority in society, meaning "all without distinction," not "all without exception." https://www.monergism.com/understanding-1-timothy-24
- *Reformed (Calvin, on v. 5):* Says the word "all" refers to classes of people, not to every individual. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/2-5.html
- *Reformed Baptist (Piper, Desiring God):* Piper takes a different Reformed line. He accepts that the verse may mean every individual, and argues for "two wills" in God. Both Calvinists and Arminians agree God doesn't save everyone because He is committed to something greater. The difference is what that is: Arminians say human self-determination, while the greater value is the manifestation of the full range of God's glory in wrath and mercy. He holds that 1 Timothy 2:4 does not settle the issue; it creates it. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/are-there-two-wills-in-god
- *Catholic:* Catholic Answers argues that God gives even unbelievers sufficient grace to respond to his call of salvation, because God wants all people to be saved. It says the verse can mean both "all kinds" and "every individual," and that Calvinists can't show it means only the first. https://www.catholic.com/audio/cot/one-christian-truth-calvinists-cant-say

**v. 5**
- Guzik: there is no valid way to God except through Jesus (compare John 14:6), and sincerity alone isn't enough. "The man Christ Jesus" shows that Christ's humanity is permanent. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-2/
- Clarke explains "mediator" as a go-between and peace-maker who reconciles two parties at odds. Barnes says there is one Mediator for kings and slaves alike, proof that God cares about the whole human race. Coffman (citing Lipscomb) notes that "man" is present tense, written after the ascension. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/2-5.html
- *Protestant objection to praying to saints:* Wesley says the verse rules out saints and angels as mediators. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-timothy-2.html Calvin rejects reading it as "one mediator" but not "the only mediator," and also rejects the split into "mediators of redemption" and "mediators of intercession." He still says Christians praying for each other doesn't conflict with Christ's role. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/2-5.html
- *Catholic:* The Catholic Encyclopedia says Christ is the Mediator in the absolute sense of the word, in a way that no one else can possibly be. It suggests keeping "mediation" for Christ and "intercession" for Mary and the saints. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08070a.htm Catholic Answers points out that the verses just before v. 5 tell Christians to intercede, and argues the saints in heaven are fellow Christians doing the same. https://www.catholic.com/tract/praying-to-the-saints

**v. 6**
- Wesley: "ransom" means an equal exchange, life for life. Because of who Christ is, the ransom was more than equivalent to all mankind. "In due time" means in God's own chosen seasons. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-timothy-2.html
- Guzik: There is enough in the work of Jesus on the cross for everyone. No one will be turned away because Jesus ran out of love or forgiveness at the cross for them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-2/
- *Reformed contrast:* Samson argues from Revelation 5 that Christ made an effectual atonement - a powerful one that achieved its desired end or goal of saving certain specific people. https://www.monergism.com/understanding-1-timothy-24

**v. 7**
- Guzik: the message Paul preached was salvation through Jesus alone. He stressed his work among Gentiles after continued rejection by Jews. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-2/
- *Catholic:* Catholic Answers notes that Paul mentions his own apostleship in the same passage, showing that Christ being "one mediator" doesn't mean nobody else has a role between God and people. https://www.catholic.com/audio/ddp/jesus-the-one-mediator

**v. 8**
- Guzik reads "everywhere" as "In every church," and not of "In every place." He says it means men are to lead public prayer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-2/
- Wesley reads it more broadly as public and private prayer: Wherever men are, there prayer should be. He calls anger, unholy actions and lack of faith the three main things that stop God hearing our prayers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-timothy-2.html

**vv. 9–10**
- Wesley is strict: the four items named are expressly forbidden by name to all women (here is no exception) professing godliness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-timothy-2.html
- Precept Austin explains these as excessive adornment (hair woven with gold and pearls) that drew attention in Paul's day and went against modesty. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-timothy-2-commentary
- Guzik reads them as things that broke propriety and moderation in that culture, and says good works are the most important adornment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-2/
- Fleming (Bridgeway) sees men tending to show off when praying in public and women tending to dress for attention, and says Paul corrects both. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/2-5.html

**v. 11**
- Guzik: "silence" is the same word as "peaceable" in v. 2. It means without arguing, not total silence, since women pray and speak in 1 Corinthians 11:5. He says "submission" is about rank and order, not worth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-2/

**v. 12: a real divide**
- *Charismatic/evangelical, complementarian (Guzik):* Women are not to have the role of teaching authority in the church. To be *under authority* is the principle; *not teaching* is the application. This applies only to home and church, not to society generally. It means those who lead the church – pastors and ruling elders – must be men. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-2/
- *Methodist (Wesley):* glosses usurping authority over the man as By public teaching. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-timothy-2.html
- Fleming: Paul doesn't think it is women's job to instruct and lead the church. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/2-5.html
- I couldn't reach any source arguing that women may be ordained, such as the Assemblies of God's position or an egalitarian scholar, so the other side of this divide is missing.

**v. 13**
- Wesley: "first" means So that woman was originally the inferior. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-timothy-2.html
- Fleming: from the beginning God gave each sex its own place. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/2-5.html

**v. 14**
- Wesley: The serpent deceived Eve: Eve did not deceive Adam, but persuaded him. He says this verse explains why a woman should not teach, as she is more easily deceived, and more easily deceives. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-timothy-2.html
- Fleming similarly says Paul thought women more easily persuaded, so more at risk of teaching error. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/2-5.html
- Enduring Word's AI summary, by contrast, says Eve's deception doesn't make women inferior. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-2/

**v. 15**
- Wesley: "she" means women in general, who share Eve's sentence in Genesis 3:16. "Saved" means carried safe through the pain and danger which that sentence entails upon them for the transgression; yea, and finally saved if they continue in faith and holiness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-timothy-2.html
- Fleming: women find their fulfilment, "salvation" and special honour in bearing children and raising them in faith, love and holiness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/2-5.html
- Enduring Word's AI summary (I couldn't read Guzik's own text here): women brought the Savior into the world, which outweighs the fall. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-timothy-2/
